rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Election Law - mandamus and the absence of a voter-initiated manual recount remedy
rows.title: Mandamus to Compel a Province-Wide Manual Recount
rows.prompt: Thirty-two registered Pangasinan voters asked COMELEC to conduct, at their expense, a province-wide manual recount of all positions in the 2022 elections. None of them was a losing candidate who had filed an election protest, and they identified no statute granting ordinary voters a right to demand revision of ballots. After COMELEC declined to conduct the recount, they petitioned for mandamus. May mandamus compel COMELEC to conduct the province-wide manual recount requested by the voters?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The voters cannot use mandamus to obtain a manual recount for which the law gives them no clear legal right.

Legal Basis: Mandamus issues only when the petitioner has a clear and complete legal right to the act demanded and the respondent has a corresponding ministerial duty to perform it. Legaspi v. COMELEC holds that no statute gives ordinary voters a right to compel a full manual recount; ballot revision is available to qualified losing candidates through an election protest.

Application: The petitioners were voters, not losing candidates pursuing an election protest, and they cited no law that required COMELEC to reopen and recount every ballot in Pangasinan. Their willingness to pay could not create either a legal right or a ministerial duty.

Conclusion: Thus, COMELEC cannot be compelled to conduct the recount because ordinary voters have no clear legal right to ballot revision and COMELEC has no corresponding ministerial duty.

COMELEC holds that no statute gives ordinary voters a right to compel a full manual recount; ballot revision is available to qualified losing candidates through an election protest.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Election Law - Section 78 cancellation for false material representation
rows.title: Cancellation of a COC for False Residency Representation
rows.prompt: Pax Ali filed a certificate of candidacy for governor of Sultan Kudarat stating that he had resided there for the required year. He continued serving as mayor of a Maguindanao municipality, kept his established domicile there, and presented no conduct showing abandonment of that domicile and acquisition of a new one in Sultan Kudarat. COMELEC found that he knowingly claimed the new residence to appear qualified. Was COMELEC correct in cancelling his certificate of candidacy under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The stated residency was a deliberately false representation concerning a qualification for governor.

Legal Basis: Section 78 permits cancellation when a candidate makes a false material representation in the certificate of candidacy with intent to deceive the electorate about eligibility. Election residence means domicile, and a new domicile requires actual residence, intent to remain, and abandonment of the former domicile; the old domicile continues until those elements concur.

Application: Pax Ali's continued exercise of mayoral office in Maguindanao and retention of his established domicile contradicted his claimed one-year Sultan Kudarat residence. Because the representation concerned a statutory qualification and was knowingly made to appear eligible, all Section 78 requisites were present.

Conclusion: Hence, COMELEC correctly cancelled Pax Ali's certificate of candidacy for false material representation.

rows.syllabus_topic: Election Law - disqualification for the election offense under Section 261(e)
rows.title: Disqualification for Indirectly Coercing an Employee to Aid a Candidacy
rows.prompt: While Noveras was governor and a candidate for vice-governor, a casual provincial employee used provincial equipment inside an LGU facility to print campaign tarpaulins bearing Noveras's name and image. The employee tried to contact his boss when discovered, and Noveras exercised official authority over his continued employment. COMELEC found that these circumstances proved indirect influence over the employee to aid Noveras's candidacy. Was Noveras's disqualification under Sections 68 and 261(e) of the Omnibus Election Code proper?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The proven circumstances support the finding that Noveras indirectly influenced a subordinate employee to aid his candidacy.

Legal Basis: Section 68 authorizes disqualification of a candidate who commits an election offense, including the conduct prohibited by Section 261(e). Under Noveras v. COMELEC, coercion or intimidation of a subordinate employee to perform election activity may be indirect and may be established by the totality of circumstantial evidence rather than an express command.

Application: A casual employee under Noveras's official authority printed materials solely benefiting Noveras, using government equipment in a government facility, and attempted to contact a boss when caught. Taken together, those facts reasonably established indirect official influence in aid of the candidacy.

Conclusion: Wherefore, Noveras was properly disqualified for the election offense established by the circumstances.

rows.syllabus_topic: Constitutional Rights - speedy disposition of administrative and quasi-judicial cases
rows.title: Speedy Disposition in a COMELEC Preliminary Investigation
rows.prompt: COMELEC began an election-offense preliminary investigation against Mayor Villanueva in 2011. Its Law Department recommended charges in 2015, but the resolution directing the filing of an information became final only in 2022. The case was not unusually complex, Villanueva did not cause the delay, and COMELEC gave no explanation for exceeding its own procedural periods by many years. Did the eleven-year preliminary investigation violate Villanueva's right to speedy disposition of cases?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The unexplained eleven-year delay was inordinate and violated the constitutional guarantee of speedy disposition.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 16 protects the speedy disposition of cases before judicial, quasi-judicial, and administrative bodies, including COMELEC preliminary investigations. When delay extends beyond governing procedural periods, the prosecution must justify it in light of the case's complexity, the parties' conduct, and resulting prejudice; unjustified inordinate delay warrants dismissal.

Application: COMELEC exceeded its own short investigation periods by roughly eleven years in a case presenting no unusual complexity, and Villanueva caused none of that lapse. Because COMELEC offered no justification after the burden shifted to it, the delay could not be considered reasonable.

Conclusion: Thus, Villanueva's constitutional right to speedy disposition was violated, requiring dismissal of the election-offense case.

rows.syllabus_topic: Constitutional Rights - zones of privacy and social-media settings
rows.title: Reasonable Expectation of Privacy in a Public Social-Media Post
rows.prompt: Rina uploaded a video to an unrestricted social-media account that anyone could view, download, and share. A classmate sent the public link to the school discipline office, which viewed only that post without bypassing a password, opening a private message, or obtaining hidden account data. Rina claims that the constitutional right to privacy barred school officials from viewing the post without her consent. Does the privacy guarantee protect Rina's deliberately public post from ordinary viewing?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Rina did not retain a reasonable expectation of privacy in content she deliberately exposed to unrestricted public viewing.

Legal Basis: Constitutional privacy protects an expectation that the person actually manifested and that society is prepared to recognize as reasonable. Under Vivares v. St. Theresa's College, social-media privacy depends materially on the user's chosen settings and voluntary disclosure; content knowingly made public is ordinarily outside that protected expectation.

Application: Rina selected an unrestricted account and permitted every internet user to view, copy, and share the video. The school used the same public link available to everyone and did not penetrate any private communication or restricted portion of her account.

Conclusion: Hence, the privacy guarantee did not prevent ordinary viewing of Rina's deliberately public post.

rows.syllabus_topic: Local Governments - adjudication of municipal boundary disputes
rows.title: Locating an Existing Municipal Boundary
rows.prompt: Isabel and Merida disputed 162.3603 hectares after Isabel placed a boundary monument near the Benabaye River. Republic Act No. 191 created Isabel from eight specifically named Merida barrios and did not include Benabaye. Old monuments, cadastral materials, and sworn historical evidence placed the statutory line along Doldol Creek, as the provincial board found. Did the provincial board act within its boundary-dispute authority by recognizing the Doldol Creek line in favor of Merida?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The board located the boundary established by the creating statute instead of altering municipal territory.

Legal Basis: In a municipal boundary dispute, the proper sanggunian determines where the boundary fixed by the local government charters actually lies by considering the creating statutes and competent geographic and historical evidence. It may locate an existing statutory line, but it cannot substantially transfer territory, which requires an Act of Congress and a plebiscite.

Application: Republic Act No. 191 omitted Benabaye from the barrios transferred to Isabel, while old monuments, cadastral records, and sworn historical evidence consistently placed the line along Doldol Creek. The board therefore identified the charter boundary rather than creating a new one.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the provincial board validly recognized Doldol Creek as the boundary because Republic Act No. 191 excluded Benabaye from Isabel and the competent historical and cadastral evidence fixed the existing statutory line there.

rows.syllabus_topic: Basic Concepts - eminent domain and compensable taking
rows.title: Compensable Taking by Permanent Government Occupation
rows.prompt: Without negotiating a sale or filing expropriation, the National Roads Agency entered Pilar's titled lot, demolished its perimeter wall, and permanently opened a public bypass across one-third of the property. Pilar never donated the occupied strip and promptly sought just compensation. The agency argues that title remains in her name and that the bypass benefits the city. Has a compensable taking occurred despite Pilar's continued paper title and the road's public benefit?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Permanent physical occupation of the strip for a public road is a compensable taking.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 9 permits private property to be taken for public use only upon payment of just compensation, while Republic Act No. 10752 implements acquisition and compensation for national infrastructure rights of way. A taking occurs when government permanently appropriates property or substantially deprives the owner of ordinary use; transfer of title is unnecessary, and public benefit does not eliminate compensation.

Application: The agency physically entered Pilar's land, destroyed an improvement, and permanently devoted a defined third of the lot to public traffic without negotiated acquisition or expropriation. Those acts excluded Pilar from possession and beneficial use of the occupied strip even though her name remained on the title.

Conclusion: Thus, Pilar suffered a compensable taking and is entitled to just compensation for the occupied property.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Constitutional Rights - prior restraint
rows.title: Prior Restraint Through Mandatory Prepublication Approval
rows.prompt: An investigative newsletter prepared a report about irregularities in city bidding. Before publication, the city licensing officer ordered the editor not to release the report unless the mayor first reviewed and approved its text. The order cited no narrowly drawn law and identified no exceptional danger that publication would create. Is the mayoral prepublication-approval order an unconstitutional prior restraint?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Conditioning publication on the mayor's advance approval is a classic and presumptively unconstitutional prior restraint.

Legal Basis: Prior restraint is official action that suppresses expression before dissemination. It bears a heavy presumption of invalidity, and government carries an exceptionally demanding burden to justify advance censorship under a narrowly applicable constitutional exception; ordinary criticism of public bidding cannot be subjected to an official licensing scheme for speech.

Application: The officer barred release before any reader could see the report and made publication depend entirely on the mayor's approval. Because the order rested on no narrow law or exceptional threatened harm, the city supplied nothing capable of overcoming the constitutional presumption.

Conclusion: Hence, the prepublication-approval order is an unconstitutional prior restraint and should be set aside.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Judicial Department - actual case or controversy
rows.title: Ripeness of a Constitutional Challenge to a Pending Bill
rows.prompt: A technology association asks the Supreme Court to invalidate a bill requiring licenses for artificial-intelligence auditors. The House approved one version, a Senate committee is considering another, and no final measure has been enacted or presented to the President. No association member has received a license denial, penalty, or compliance order. Is there an actual and ripe case or controversy for judicial review?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The petition asks for an advisory opinion about a contingent proposal rather than an enforceable legal dispute.

Legal Basis: Judicial review under Article VIII requires an actual case or controversy involving concrete, opposing legal claims and an existing or imminent injury susceptible of judicial resolution. A challenge is unripe when it depends on uncertain future legislative events, and public importance cannot authorize an advisory opinion on a bill.

Application: The two chambers had not agreed on statutory text, the President had not acted, and no government officer had enforced any obligation against a member. Both the eventual law and any injury therefore depended on political events that might never occur.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the Court must dismiss the petition for want of an actual and ripe controversy because the challenged measure remains an unenacted bill and no association member faces an existing or imminent injury.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Executive Department - factual basis for martial law
rows.title: Rebellion Without Complete Territorial Control
rows.prompt: An armed organization seized three municipal halls, burned police stations, freed detainees, and announced that it was replacing national authority across the province. Intelligence reports showed coordinated attacks on power facilities and the flight of local officials. The President proclaimed martial law in the province for sixty days and reported to Congress within forty-eight hours. The challengers concede these facts but argue that the rebels had not gained complete control of the province. Must rebels first obtain complete territorial control before the President may proclaim martial law?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Complete rebel control of territory is not a constitutional prerequisite to a martial-law proclamation.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 18 permits the President to proclaim martial law for not more than sixty days when actual invasion or rebellion exists and public safety requires it. Judicial review examines the factual sufficiency of those two predicates; the Constitution does not require that insurgents first succeed in governing or controlling the whole affected territory.

Application: Seizure of government buildings, attacks on police and infrastructure, release of detainees, displacement of officials, and an announced effort to replace lawful authority objectively indicate actual rebellion and a public-safety danger. The rebels' failure to control every part of the province does not negate those facts.

Conclusion: Thus, the proclamation is not invalid for lack of complete territorial control because actual rebellion and the needs of public safety—not successful rebel governance—are the constitutional predicates.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Constitutional Rights - writ of amparo
rows.title: Amparo Relief for a Concrete Threat of Enforced Disappearance
rows.prompt: After organizer Lia criticized a security operation, uniformed personnel repeatedly visited her home, photographed her family, and told neighbors that she would disappear. An official social-media page displayed her photograph beside an armed-group emblem. Lia preserved the posts and presented sworn witnesses to the visits and threats. She remains physically free but alleges an imminent State-linked threat of enforced disappearance. May Lia seek a writ of amparo before an actual abduction occurs?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Amparo may protect against a substantially proven threat of enforced disappearance before the threatened abduction is completed.

Legal Basis: The Rule on the Writ of Amparo covers unlawful acts or omissions of public officials or private persons that violate or threaten life, liberty, or security in connection with an extralegal killing or enforced disappearance. The petitioner must establish the covered violation or threat by substantial evidence, but need not await consummation of the feared harm.

Application: Uniformed visits, surveillance of Lia's family, an express warning that she would disappear, and official online branding tied the danger to State actors and to enforced disappearance. Her preserved posts and sworn witnesses provide concrete evidence beyond an unparticularized fear.

Conclusion: Hence, Lia may seek amparo before an actual abduction occurs because substantial evidence shows a State-linked threat of enforced disappearance.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Constitutional Rights - particularity requirement for search warrants
rows.title: Particularity of Things Described in a Search Warrant
rows.prompt: Investigators established probable cause for falsification of one identified government bid dated 12 March and identified the desktop computer used to prepare it. The warrant nevertheless authorized seizure from a three-storey office of all papers, computers, phones, storage devices, and other objects showing any unlawful activity. Officers used that language to take payroll ledgers, family phones, and unrelated project records. Does the warrant satisfy the constitutional particularity requirement?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The open-ended authorization created a general warrant instead of limiting the search to objectively identifiable evidence of the specified offense.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 2 requires a search warrant to particularly describe the place to be searched and the things to be seized for the one specific offense supported by probable cause. The description must confine officer discretion; authority to seize anything suggesting any illegality is impermissibly general.

Application: Probable cause concerned one dated bid and a known desktop, yet the warrant covered every record and device in the office that officers might associate with any unlawful activity. That breadth enabled seizure of family phones, payroll files, and projects unrelated to the falsification alleged.

rows.prompt: An international health conference adopted a nonbinding recommendation encouraging States to prohibit advertising of high-sugar food. rows.title: Custodial Admissions Obtained Through a Police-Arranged Confrontation

rows.title: Legislative Inquiry Conducted Without Duly Published Rules
rows.prompt: A Senate committee summoned Lina to an inquiry during a new Congress. The committee's prior rules of procedure had not been published for that Congress, and replacement rules were uploaded only after Lina appeared. Acting under the unpublished rules, the committee cited her in contempt and ordered her detained for refusing to answer. Is the contempt detention valid despite the absence of duly published governing rules when the hearing occurred?

Answer: No. Legislative contempt cannot rest on an inquiry conducted without the duly published rules required by the Constitution.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 21 permits each House or its committees to conduct inquiries in aid of legislation only in accordance with duly published rules of procedure. Application: Lina appeared when no governing inquiry rules for the Congress had been duly published, yet the committee invoked those unavailable procedures to detain her. Uploading replacement rules only after her appearance supplied no prior notice and could not cure the constitutional defect.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the contempt order and resulting detention are invalid for want of duly published rules.

rows.title: Equal Protection and Full-Fleet Zero-Emission Classification
rows.prompt: To reduce urban emissions, a city ordinance grants a five-year registration-fee rebate to public-transport operators whose entire active fleet uses zero-emission vehicles. Transport data show materially greater air-quality gains from full-fleet conversion. Every operator may qualify at any time during the transition, and every qualifying operator receives the same rebate. Answer: Yes. The classification rests on a substantial and relevant distinction and operates equally and prospectively within the defined class.

Legal Basis: Equal protection permits classification when it rests on substantial distinctions, is germane to the law's purpose, is not confined to existing conditions, and applies equally to every member of the class. The five-year window allows any operator to enter the class, and the ordinance grants the same rebate to every operator meeting the objective zero-emission condition.

Conclusion: Thus, the full-fleet classification satisfies equal protection because it substantially advances emissions reduction, remains open to every operator during the transition, and treats all qualifying operators alike.

rows.syllabus_topic: Basic Concepts - permissible delegation of administrative implementation
rows.title: Delegation Guided by a Complete Law and Sufficient Standard
rows.prompt: Congress enacted a law making battery producers bear collection costs, identifying the covered products and liable persons, and directing an environmental board to compute an annual charge from collection volume, audited disposal cost, and toxicity weights fixed in the statute. After notice and hearing, the board calculated the charge using only those factors. VoltWorks argues that Congress had to state the final peso amount itself. Did Congress unconstitutionally delegate legislative power to the environmental board?

Answer: No. Congress made the law and confined the board to calculating its charge under legislatively fixed standards.

Legal Basis: Delegation to an administrative agency is valid when the statute is complete in its essential terms and supplies a sufficient standard that guides and limits implementation. Congress must determine policy and legal consequences, but it may authorize an agency to ascertain facts, apply technical formulas, and fill in operational details.

Application: The statute selected the regulated products and liable producers, imposed the cost obligation, and prescribed measurable volume, disposal-cost, and toxicity variables. The board could not choose a different policy or subject; it merely calculated the amount from the formula after the required hearing.

Conclusion: Hence, the board exercised permissible administrative implementation rather than delegated lawmaking power.

rows.title: State Immunity in a Contract Serving a Sovereign Function
rows.prompt: The Department of External Relations contracted with Harborstone Builders to repair an official diplomatic residence used in conducting foreign relations. The agreement contained no waiver of immunity, and Harborstone identified no statute consenting to suit. Legal Basis: Article XVI, Section 3 declares that the State may not be sued without its consent. Conclusion: Wherefore, the direct suit against the Republic is not maintainable because repairing an official diplomatic residence served a sovereign function and neither law nor contract waived State immunity.

rows.title: Administrative Due Process Through Written Submissions
rows.prompt: A bank received an administrative charge for inaccurate regulatory reports, the supporting audit worksheets, and thirty days to file a verified answer with an expert report. rows.title: Administrative Issuance Cannot Create a Franchise Tax
rows.prompt: Before Republic Act No. 11590, an offshore POGO licensee operated its gaming website abroad, accepted only foreign players abroad, and placed and paid all wagers abroad. Legal Basis: The power to impose a tax is legislative, and every tax must rest on a clear statutory grant. Conclusion: Wherefore, the BIR could not validly impose the franchise tax through the circular before Republic Act No. 11590.

rows.title: Material Concealment Unrelated to the Cause of Death
rows.prompt: When applying for life insurance, Ruben was asked whether a physician had diagnosed a heart condition during the previous five years. rows.title: No Tax Exemption by Implication
rows.prompt: Aurora Learning Network's charter authorizes local governments to grant incentives promoting educational broadcasting but does not exempt Aurora from local franchise or business taxes. Conclusion: Hence, Aurora remains subject to the city tax because no law clearly exempts it.

rows.title: No Exclusion Solely for Electronic Form
rows.prompt: Aster Components sues on a supply agreement negotiated through company email. It offers the native message files, server logs showing that the records remained unaltered, and records-custodian testimony authenticating the messages and confirming their accessibility for later reference. The buyer objects only that no paper original exists. May the court exclude the authenticated agreement solely because it is electronic and has no paper counterpart?

Answer: No. Electronic form and the absence of a paper counterpart are not independent grounds for denying legal effect or admissibility.

Legal Basis: Sections 6, 7, and 12 of the Electronic Commerce Act recognize electronic data messages and documents and prohibit exclusion solely because of electronic form. Because the buyer's sole objection is the missing paper original, that objection attacks electronic form rather than any unproved statutory safeguard.

Conclusion: Thus, the court may not exclude the authenticated agreement solely for lacking a paper counterpart.

rows.title: Presumption of Carrier Negligence for Damaged Cargo
rows.prompt: A shipper delivered sealed cartons of medical glass to Ocean Crest Lines in sound condition, as shown by a clean bill of lading and loading photographs. At destination, many cartons were crushed and wet. The carrier offered no loading plan, stowage record, weather log, or witness explaining the damage and merely referred to ordinary sea risks. Does proof of good delivery and damaged arrival create a rebuttable presumption that the common carrier was negligent?

Answer: Yes. The unexplained damage after receipt in good order raises the statutory presumption against the common carrier.

Legal Basis: Articles 1733 to 1735 of the Civil Code require common carriers to exercise extraordinary diligence over goods. Once the shipper proves delivery to the carrier in good condition and loss or damage before proper delivery, fault or negligence is presumed; the carrier must then prove an enumerated exempt cause and the diligence required by law.

Application: The clean bill of lading and photographs established that the medical glass entered Ocean Crest's custody undamaged, while destination inspection showed crushing and water exposure. Ocean Crest identified no specific exempt cause and produced no handling or voyage evidence capable of proving extraordinary diligence.

Conclusion: Hence, the unrebutted presumption of carrier negligence applies to the damaged cargo.

rows.title: Piercing the Corporate Veil to Defeat Fraudulent Evasion
rows.prompt: Northbay Foods lost a final labor judgment. The next day, its sole shareholder formed Cedar Kitchens, transferred all Northbay equipment to Cedar without consideration, continued the same premises, managers, workers, customers, and bank signatories, and left Northbay assetless. Internal messages state that Cedar was created so the employees could collect nothing. May the corporate veil be pierced to prevent evasion of the labor judgment?

Answer: Yes. Cedar's separate personality was used as the instrument for a deliberate scheme to defeat an existing lawful obligation.

Legal Basis: A corporation ordinarily has a personality separate from its shareholders and related entities, but courts may pierce the veil when complete domination is used to perpetrate fraud, evade an existing obligation, or justify a wrong, and that misuse proximately causes the claimant's injury. Application: The sole shareholder moved every operating asset without consideration immediately after final judgment, preserved the same business under Cedar, and left Northbay unable to pay. The internal messages expressly connected the new corporation and transfer to the plan to defeat the employees' adjudged claims.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the veil may be pierced to prevent the fraudulent evasion of the labor judgment.

rows.title: Stay of Execution After a Rehabilitation Commencement Order
rows.prompt: A rehabilitation court issued and published a commencement order for Meridian Fabricators. Despite notice, a machinery supplier continued a collection case filed before rehabilitation, obtained a writ, and directed the sheriff to levy Meridian's production line. The supplier identified no statutory exception and argued only that its earlier filing allowed execution to finish. May the supplier continue levy and execution after the commencement order?

Answer: No. The commencement order stays enforcement and execution against the debtor regardless of the collection case's earlier filing.

Legal Basis: Section 16 of the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act stays all actions or proceedings to enforce claims against the debtor and suspends execution, attachment, and other processes against its property upon commencement of rehabilitation, subject only to the statutory exceptions. Application: The supplier seeks to enforce a precommencement monetary claim by seizing Meridian's own production equipment after receiving notice of the order. Earlier filing is not a statutory exception, and removing machinery needed for operations would defeat the asset-preservation purpose of the rehabilitation process.

Conclusion: Thus, levy and execution must stop, and the supplier must present its claim in rehabilitation, because the commencement order stays enforcement and no statutory exception applies.

rows.title: Liability of a Purported Partner by Estoppel

Conclusion: Hence, Sela is liable to Vista as a partner by estoppel for the induced credit transaction.

rows.title: Agent's Prohibition Against Acquiring an Adverse Title
rows.prompt: The Tad-y spouses authorized PNB under their mortgage to advance real-property taxes and act to protect the mortgaged lots. When the lots were sold for tax delinquency, PNB bought them at auction, later accepted full payment of the spouses' loans without foreclosure, and then claimed the lots as its own. May PNB retain a title acquired adversely to the spouses while acting within that agency?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. PNB may not retain the tax-sale title against the spouses.

Legal Basis: An agent occupies a fiduciary position and may not, with respect to property covered by the agency, acquire or assert an interest adverse to the principal. Application: PNB's authority to advance taxes existed to protect the spouses' mortgaged property, not to appropriate it. PNB used that position to buy the lots, accepted full loan payment without foreclosure, and then asserted ownership against its principals.

Conclusion: Hence, PNB holds the acquired title in constructive trust and must reconvey the lots to the spouses.

rows.syllabus_topic: Marriage — Article 26 Recognition of Foreign Divorce
rows.title: Recognition of a Foreign Divorce Obtained by Mutual Agreement
rows.prompt: Maia, a Filipina, married Kenji, a Japanese citizen, in Manila. They later obtained a divorce by mutual agreement in Japan. Maia presented an authenticated divorce certificate, the official Japanese family registry, and a properly authenticated official publication of Japanese divorce law establishing that the divorce is valid and capacitates Kenji to remarry. Answer: No. Article 26 does not categorically exclude a valid foreign divorce obtained by mutual agreement.

Legal Basis: Article 26, paragraph 2 is a corrective exception to the nationality principle, designed to prevent the inequity of leaving the Filipino spouse married while the alien spouse is free to remarry. Its operation turns on the existence of a divorce valid under the alien spouse's national law that capacitates that spouse to remarry, not on who initiated the divorce or whether its foreign modality was adversarial, judicial, administrative, or consensual. Once those facts are proved, the Filipino spouse may obtain recognition and corresponding capacity to remarry.

That law validates the mutual-agreement divorce and frees Kenji to remarry, so the absence of an adversarial foreign judgment does not defeat Article 26.

Conclusion: Hence, the consensual modality does not bar recognition because Maia proved a valid foreign divorce that capacitates her alien spouse to remarry.

rows.title: Effect of a Co-owner's Sale of the Entire Property
rows.prompt: Ada, Ben, and Cora own an unpartitioned farm in equal shares. Without authority from the others, Ben sold the entire farm to Victor, who knew the title named all three co-owners. rows.title: Nonmarital Grandchildren's Right of Representation
rows.prompt: Tomas died intestate after his legitimate son Paolo had predeceased him. Paolo's two nonmarital children proved their filiation through civil-registry records and claimed the share Paolo would have inherited from Tomas. rows.title: Full Payment as a Suspensive Condition in a Contract to Sell
rows.prompt: Orchid Logistics agreed to buy a warehouse under a contract to sell that expressly retained title in the owner and required full payment before execution of an absolute deed. Conclusion: Hence, the owner may refuse conveyance without first obtaining Article 1191 rescission because Orchid’s failure to pay the balance prevented the full-payment suspensive condition from occurring.

rows.title: Employer Liability for an Employee's Quasi-delict

rows.title: Enforcement of a Right of First Refusal
rows.prompt: Ramon's lease promised to offer the premises first to lessee Lumen if Ramon decided to sell. Ramon accepted Petra's definite offer of PHP 12 million without notifying Lumen, although Petra knew the registered lease contained the clause. Lumen promptly offered to match Petra's exact payment terms. Is Ramon correct that the clause is unenforceable as an option lacking separate consideration?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The right of first refusal is not an unsupported option.

Legal Basis: A right of first refusal is distinct from an option because it does not compel an owner to sell at a pre-agreed price; it requires the owner, once genuinely deciding to sell on definite terms, to offer the property first to the holder on those same terms. Separate option consideration is therefore not indispensable to that covenant.

Application: Ramon's acceptance of Petra's definite price and schedule triggered Lumen's contractual priority. Lumen matched those exact terms promptly, and Petra's notice of the registered lease prevents treating the bypass as an innocent purchase.

Conclusion: Hence, Ramon cannot defeat the triggered right of first refusal by relabeling it as an unsupported option.

rows.syllabus_topic: Sales — Legal Redemption by a Co-owner
rows.title: Judicial Review of a Grossly Excessive Redemption Price
rows.prompt: Joel sold his undivided half of co-owned land to outsider Karla for a stated PHP 5 million and gave co-owner Inez written notice. Inez timely sought redemption but tendered PHP 3 million, alleging with supporting comparable sales that the deed price was simulated and grossly excessive to defeat redemption. Is Karla correct that the stated deed price is conclusive and automatically defeats Inez's redemption?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. A grossly excessive stated price may be judicially examined.

Legal Basis: Article 1620 grants a co-owner legal redemption when another co-owner sells an undivided share to a third person. Although the redeemer generally reimburses the buyer's price and lawful expenses, a stated price alleged and proved to be simulated or grossly excessive is not conclusive; the court may determine the reasonable redemption amount.

Application: Inez invoked redemption within the statutory period and identified concrete comparable sales supporting her claim that the PHP 5 million figure was artificially inflated. That evidence warrants adjudication of the lawful reimbursement rather than automatic forfeiture.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the deed price is not conclusive and the court may determine the lawful redemption amount because Inez timely alleged simulation or gross excessiveness and supported the challenge with comparable sales.

rows.syllabus_topic: Obligations and Contracts — Mutuality
rows.title: Mutuality and a Lender's Unilateral Interest-rate Reset
rows.prompt: A loan fixed nine percent interest for one year, then allowed Harbor Bank to impose any replacement rate it chose whenever it considered market conditions unfavorable. Celso could neither reject nor negotiate a posted reset, and the clause identified no independent index or formula. Harbor Bank later imposed twenty-two percent without Celso's conformity. Is the unilateral twenty-two percent reset enforceable?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The unilateral reset violates the mutuality of contracts.

Legal Basis: Article 1308 requires a contract to bind both parties and prohibits leaving its validity or compliance to the will of only one party. A lender may adjust interest through an agreed objective formula or a rate accepted by the borrower, but it may not reserve exclusive power to select and impose the binding rate.

Application: Harbor Bank alone determined when conditions were unfavorable and what replacement rate would apply. The contract supplied no external index, reciprocal choice, or later assent by Celso to the twenty-two percent figure.

Conclusion: Thus, the bank's unilaterally selected twenty-two percent rate is unenforceable for lack of mutuality.

rows.syllabus_topic: Obligations — Solidary Liability
rows.title: Creditor's Right to Collect the Whole from One Solidary Debtor
rows.prompt: Rho, Sigma, and Tau signed an undertaking expressly making them solidarily liable for a PHP 3 million debt to Una. At maturity, Una demanded the entire unpaid amount from Sigma alone. The agreement contains no benefit of excussion and does not require the creditor to divide the claim or exhaust the other debtors first. May Una collect the whole enforceable debt from Sigma alone?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Una may demand the whole debt from Sigma.

Legal Basis: Under Article 1216, a creditor may proceed against any one, some, or all solidary debtors simultaneously or successively until the obligation is fully collected. Express solidarity removes any requirement that the creditor divide the demand proportionately or first exhaust the property of the other solidary debtors.

Application: The written undertaking expressly created solidarity, and no clause granted Sigma a benefit of excussion or imposed an order of collection. Una may therefore select Sigma for the entire unpaid balance at maturity.

Conclusion: Hence, Una may collect the entire enforceable debt from Sigma alone because their undertaking expressly made each debtor solidarily liable and imposed no order of collection.

rows.syllabus_topic: Labor Standards — Proof of Wage and Benefit Payment
rows.title: Employer's Burden to Prove Payment of Wages and Benefits
rows.prompt: Three overseas nursing aides claimed underpayment under their approved contracts. The employers controlled the payroll records but produced sheets containing identical signatures, repeated erasures, unchanged amounts despite admitted absences, and entries bearing a former worker's signature months after she had left Saudi Arabia. No independent remittance or credible payroll evidence corroborated payment. Did the employers discharge their burden to prove correct payment?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The employers failed to prove correct payment.

Legal Basis: When employees allege underpayment or nonpayment of wages and contractually mandated benefits, the employer bears the burden of proving payment because payrolls, remittances, time records, and personnel files are within its custody and control. Dubious or unauthenticated records with material signs of fabrication do not constitute substantial evidence of payment.

Application: The employers relied on payroll sheets marked by duplicated signatures, erasures, implausibly uniform amounts, and entries for a worker who had already departed. Without credible corroborating remittances or authentic records, those documents do not prove payment.

Conclusion: Thus, the defective payroll sheets did not satisfy the employers' evidentiary burden.

rows.syllabus_topic: Labor Relations — Interpretation and Enforcement of a CBA
rows.title: CBA Benefit Limited to the Defined Bargaining Unit
rows.prompt: A CBA grants the regular rank-and-file bargaining unit an eighteen percent share of the cooperative's net surplus. The cooperative separately promised the same percentage to managers, supervisors, and confidential employees, then charged those payments against the CBA pool and reduced the rank-and-file allocation. May the cooperative dilute the bargained share by including employees excluded from the CBA's defined unit?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The cooperative may not dilute the bargaining unit's share.

Legal Basis: A collective bargaining agreement is the law between the parties and must be read as a whole and performed in good faith. When its scope provisions clearly define the covered bargaining unit, a negotiated economic benefit belongs to that unit; management may grant outsiders separate bonuses but may not charge them against the CBA benefit.

Application: The CBA expressly covers regular rank-and-file employees, while managers, supervisors, and confidential employees fall outside that unit. Debiting their separate grants from the same pool reduces the precise eighteen percent benefit the union negotiated.

Conclusion: Hence, the cooperative may not dilute the bargained share because the CBA assigns the eighteen-percent benefit exclusively to the defined rank-and-file bargaining unit.

rows.syllabus_topic: Termination — Abandonment
rows.title: Abandonment Requires a Clear Intent to Sever Employment
rows.prompt: A restaurant worker reported for his usual shift but was denied entry and removed from the schedule. Within five days, he filed an illegal-dismissal complaint asking for reinstatement. The restaurant admits it sent no return-to-work directive and identifies no act showing that the worker intended to end the employment relationship. Did the worker abandon his job?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The worker did not abandon his employment.

Legal Basis: Abandonment requires both an unjustified failure to report for work and a clear, overt, and unequivocal intention to sever the employer-employee relationship. The employer bears the burden of proving that intention, and an employee's prompt filing of an illegal-dismissal complaint seeking reinstatement is ordinarily inconsistent with abandonment.

Application: The worker attempted to report but the restaurant barred him and removed his schedule. His complaint followed within five days and expressly sought reinstatement, while the restaurant proved no communication or conduct showing a desire to quit.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the evidence shows exclusion from work and a wish to return, not abandonment.

rows.title: Mandatory Third-doctor Referral in a Seafarer Disability Claim
rows.prompt: A seafarer was repatriated for diabetes and hypertension. Within the contractual period, the company-designated physician issued a complete and final fit-to-work assessment. The seafarer's private doctor later declared him disabled, but the seafarer neither disclosed the conflict for referral nor requested a mutually chosen third doctor before filing his claim. Is the seafarer entitled to permanent total disability benefits despite omitting the third-doctor procedure?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The timely company-designated physician's assessment controls.

Legal Basis: When a seafarer's physician disagrees with a timely, definite, and medically supported assessment by the company-designated physician, the POEA employment contract requires referral to a third doctor jointly selected by the parties. Absent a recognized justification, the seafarer's failure to initiate that conflict-resolution procedure makes the company assessment binding.

Application: The company physician issued a final fit-to-work assessment within the governing period, and the private doctor supplied the contrary opinion that created the contractual conflict. The seafarer bypassed the agreed third-doctor mechanism without any stated exception.

Conclusion: Thus, the unexcused failure to seek third-doctor referral defeats the disability claim based solely on the private assessment.

rows.syllabus_topic: Termination — Fraud or Willful Breach of Trust
rows.title: Willful Breach of Trust by a Managerial Employee
rows.prompt: Procurement supervisor Leah concealed that an accredited supplier was wholly owned by her spouse, fabricated two competing quotations, and steered three contracts to that supplier at prices thirty-five percent above prevailing bids. She admits the concealment and fabricated quotations but notes that no criminal judgment or final loss computation exists. Is there substantive just cause for dismissal based on willful breach of trust, assuming due process?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Leah's acts constitute willful breach of trust.

Legal Basis: Fraud or willful breach of trust is a just cause when an employee occupying a position of confidence commits, by substantial evidence, an intentional and work-related act that makes continued trust untenable. Application: Leah controlled vendor accreditation and certified competitive canvasses, yet deliberately hid her household's financial interest and fabricated quotations to defeat those safeguards. Those admitted acts directly abuse the special confidence attached to her procurement authority.

Conclusion: Hence, the employer may dismiss Leah for the proven, work-related willful breach of trust.

rows.title: Employer's Evidentiary Burden in Retrenchment
rows.prompt: Philphos retrenched long-serving rank-and-file employees to reduce costs. Conclusion: Wherefore, the unsubstantiated cost-saving measure was not a valid retrenchment.

rows.syllabus_topic: Employer-Employee Relationship — Control Test
rows.title: Control Test for an Employer-Employee Relationship
rows.prompt: Licensed physiotherapist Carina rents a room from a wellness center, chooses her patients and schedule, fixes her professional fees, and decides each treatment method. The center enforces building hours, sanitation, patient-safety rules, a dress code, and review of advertisements, but prescribes no therapy method or work quota. Does the center's limited regulation establish an employer-employee relationship under the control test?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The center does not exercise the legally decisive control.

Legal Basis: Under the control test, an employer-employee relationship exists when the putative employer reserves the right to control not merely the desired result but also the means and methods by which the work is performed. Rules that protect premises, safety, or public-facing standards do not establish employment when professional methods remain independently controlled.

Application: Carina alone selects patients, sets her schedule and fees, and determines how therapy is performed. The center's hours, sanitation, safety, dress, and advertising rules regulate the facility and presentation, not her therapeutic means or methods.

Conclusion: Thus, the center's neutral facility rules do not satisfy the control test for employment.

rows.syllabus_topic: Recruitment and Placement — Illegal Recruitment Distinguished from Estafa
rows.title: Separate Liability for Illegal Recruitment and Estafa
rows.prompt: Unlicensed Mira promised Carlo an overseas hotel job, displayed fabricated employer emails, and collected PHP 90,000 in placement fees, although she submitted no application and spent the money. The licensing authority confirms that she never possessed recruitment authority, and Carlo proves reliance and pecuniary damage. May Mira be convicted of both illegal recruitment and estafa if every element is proved?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Separate convictions may be imposed for the two offenses.

Legal Basis: Illegal recruitment punishes the undertaking of recruitment or placement activities without the license or authority required by law. Estafa separately punishes prior or simultaneous deceit that induces reliance and causes damage. Because each offense requires an element the other does not, one does not absorb the other even when both arise from one transaction.

Application: Mira performed recruitment acts without authority, satisfying the element unique to illegal recruitment. Her fabricated employer emails separately induced Carlo to part with PHP 90,000 and caused actual loss, supplying deceit, reliance, and damage for estafa.

Conclusion: Hence, upon proof of every element, Mira may be convicted of both illegal recruitment and estafa because each offense contains an element the other does not and neither absorbs the other.

Management controlled workloads, renewals, and promotions but claimed each act was an ordinary business decision. Does the totality of AIM's conduct constitute unfair labor practice by interference with self-organization?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The coordinated anti-union conduct constitutes unfair labor practice.

Legal Basis: Article 259(a) makes it employer unfair labor practice to interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in exercising the right to self-organization. Acts facially within management prerogative lose that protection when, viewed in their totality with preceding and subsequent circumstances, substantial evidence shows that anti-union purpose motivated discrimination or disadvantage.

Application: AIM expressly rejected the organization and then used powers over workload, scholarship, and promotion against identified leaders and registrants while referring to their union activity. Taken together, those linked acts reveal interference rather than unrelated neutral decisions.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the totality of AIM's discriminatory conduct unlawfully interfered with the faculty members' right to organize.

rows.syllabus_topic: Termination — Constructive Dismissal
rows.title: Constructive Dismissal Through a Bad-faith Demotion and Transfer
rows.prompt: After supervisor Mara reported falsified inventory, Northline reassigned her as a clerk sixty-five kilometers away, removed her supervisory duties and PHP 6,000 allowance, and cited only management discretion despite a nearby supervisor vacancy. Mara protested, received no explanation, and resigned after two weeks because of the new conditions. Was Mara constructively dismissed?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Northline constructively dismissed Mara.

Legal Basis: Management may transfer an employee only for a genuine business reason, in good faith, and without demotion, diminution of pay or benefits, discrimination, or unreasonable prejudice. A transfer that crosses those limits and makes continued employment objectively unreasonable constitutes constructive dismissal even without an express termination notice.

Application: Northline replaced Mara's supervisory work with clerical duties, removed a recurring allowance, and imposed a distant assignment without operational explanation despite a nearby vacancy. The timing after her report and the employer's silence support bad faith and unreasonable prejudice.

Conclusion: Thus, the demotional, benefit-reducing, and unjustified transfer amounted to constructive dismissal.

rows.title: Labor-only Contracting Despite Registration and Paid-up Capital
rows.prompt: Registered contractor PackPro, with PHP 5 million paid-up capital, supplied packaging workers to Harvest but provided no equipment, supervisors, independent method, or defined result. Harvest trained them, set schedules and stations, approved leave, dictated methods, evaluated performance, and could remove any worker. PackPro merely processed payroll from Harvest's advances for a per-worker fee. Is PackPro engaged in labor-only contracting?

Answer: Yes. PackPro is a labor-only contractor.

Legal Basis: Registration and the prescribed paid-up capital are not conclusive proof of legitimate job contracting. Application: PackPro contributed no work system, project supervision, tools, or independent result and acted only as a payroll conduit. Harvest controlled virtually every operational aspect of the workers' performance, including training, schedules, methods, evaluation, leave, and removal.

Conclusion: Hence, PackPro is engaged in labor-only contracting because it supplied labor without an independent business or defined result while Harvest controlled the workers’ means and methods.

rows.title: Statutory Wage Distortion After a Wage-order Increase
rows.prompt: A regional wage order increased entry-level pay at a Cebu plant by PHP 60. The plant's established wage grades previously maintained a PHP 70 difference between entry employees and senior operators, but the mandated increase reduced that difference to PHP 10 without any corresponding adjustment. Does the severe contraction of the established same-region wage hierarchy constitute wage distortion?

Answer: Yes. The wage-order increase produced statutory wage distortion.

Legal Basis: Wage distortion exists when a legally prescribed wage increase eliminates or severely contracts intentional quantitative differences in wage or salary rates between employee groups in the same region, thereby disrupting the established hierarchy based on skill, length of service, or other logical distinctions. The law then requires correction through the applicable grievance or statutory procedure.

Application: The regional order affected the Cebu entry rate and reduced an established PHP 70 grade differential to only PHP 10. That severe contraction materially disrupts the plant's defined hierarchy between entry employees and senior operators.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the wage-order increase created a wage distortion because it reduced the plant’s established same-region differential between entry employees and senior operators from PHP 70 to PHP 10.

rows.syllabus_topic: Kinds of Employment — Probationary Employment
rows.title: Termination of a Probationary Employee for Unmet Disclosed Standards
rows.prompt: Clinic Orenda hired therapist Mae for six months and gave her signed copies of reasonable patient-safety and documentation standards on her first day. Monthly evaluations recorded repeated failures. Before the probationary period expired, Orenda served written notice terminating her solely for failure to qualify, without using the twin-notice procedure for a disciplinary offense. Was the probationary termination valid?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The termination was valid on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: A probationary employee may be terminated for failure to meet reasonable qualification standards made known at the time of engagement. When the sole ground is nonqualification rather than a just-cause disciplinary offense, the employer must give timely written notice of termination stating that ground, but the full twin-notice procedure for misconduct is not required.

Application: Orenda disclosed objective standards when Mae began work, repeatedly documented her failure to satisfy them, and notified her in writing before probation ended. The notice relied only on nonqualification and did not accuse her of separate misconduct.

Conclusion: Thus, Orenda validly ended Mae's probationary employment for failure to meet disclosed reasonable standards.

rows.syllabus_topic: Termination — Statutory Due Process and Agabon Damages
rows.title: Effect of Procedural Defect on an Otherwise Valid Just-cause Dismissal
rows.prompt: Authenticated records proved that cashier Elise altered deposit slips and diverted PHP 180,000. Metro Transit nevertheless dismissed her after a vague three-hour text demand, without identifying the transactions, providing the requested records, or giving a meaningful opportunity to answer. The serious misconduct is established, but statutory procedure was not observed. Does the procedural defect alone make the otherwise justified dismissal illegal?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The proven just cause keeps the dismissal effective.

Legal Basis: A just-cause dismissal requires a first written notice specifying the charge, a meaningful opportunity to respond, and a second notice communicating the decision. When the employer proves a valid just cause but violates that statutory procedure, the dismissal remains effective; the procedural breach is remedied by nominal damages under the Agabon doctrine, ordinarily PHP 30,000.

Application: Elise's authenticated alterations and diversion establish substantive just cause, while Metro's vague text, withheld records, and three-hour deadline denied meaningful notice and response. The two findings coexist, so the defect warrants nominal damages rather than reinstatement or backwages.

Conclusion: Hence, Elise is not entitled to reinstatement and full backwages solely for the procedural violation, although nominal damages are due.

rows.syllabus_topic: Labor Standards — Equal Pay for Work of Equal Value
rows.title: Equal Pay for Substantially Equal Work
rows.prompt: A private school pays locally hired teachers lower base salaries than foreign-hired teachers. Both groups teach identical subjects, possess comparable licenses and experience, carry the same loads, and work under the same conditions. The school relies only on nationality and recruitment origin, while reimbursing documented relocation costs separately. Is the base-salary classification valid?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The nationality-based base-pay distinction is invalid.

Legal Basis: Employees who perform substantially equal work under similar conditions and possess comparable qualifications, skill, effort, and responsibility must receive equal pay unless the employer proves a real and job-related distinction. Nationality or foreign-hire status alone cannot justify lower compensation for equivalent work, although actual relocation costs may be separately reimbursed.

Application: The local and foreign-hired teachers have comparable credentials, assignments, responsibilities, evaluations, and working conditions. Separate relocation reimbursement addresses the foreign hires' documented expense and supplies no job-related basis for a permanent difference in base salary.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the base-salary classification is invalid because the two teacher groups perform substantially equal work under the same conditions and the school proved no job-related distinction.

rows.syllabus_topic: Management Prerogative — Transfer of Employees
rows.title: Valid Transfer Pursuant to Management Prerogative
rows.prompt: A bank closed one branch when its lease expired and transferred teller Juno three kilometers to the surviving branch under criteria applied to all affected staff. Her rank, salary, benefits, schedule, and duties remained unchanged, and the bank offered temporary transportation. No punitive or discriminatory motive appears, but Juno prefers her former coworkers. Is the transfer unlawful?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The transfer is a lawful exercise of management prerogative.

Legal Basis: Management may transfer an employee for a legitimate business purpose when the reassignment is made in good faith and causes no demotion, diminution of salary or benefits, discrimination, or unreasonable inconvenience or prejudice. An employee's personal preference does not override an otherwise fair and necessary operational transfer.

Application: The expired lease and branch consolidation provide a documented business reason, the same criteria governed all affected workers, and Juno retained every material employment term. A three-kilometer move with temporary transport is not unreasonable prejudice.

Conclusion: Thus, Juno’s transfer is lawful because the branch closure supplied a legitimate business reason and the good-faith reassignment caused no demotion, diminution, discrimination, or unreasonable prejudice.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Labor Relations — Individual Consequences of an Illegal Strike
rows.title: Ordinary Member's Peaceful Participation in an Illegal Strike
rows.prompt: A final judgment declared a union strike illegal for statutory noncompliance. Nestor, an ordinary union member, peacefully joined the picket line but committed no violence, coercion, obstruction, or property damage. His employer dismissed him solely because he participated in the illegal strike, without alleging any individual illegal act. Was Nestor's dismissal valid?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Peaceful participation alone does not justify dismissing an ordinary member.

Legal Basis: An ordinary union member does not lose employment merely by joining a strike later declared illegal. Dismissal requires individualized proof that the particular member committed an illegal act during the strike; the collective illegality of the concerted activity cannot replace proof of the employee's own prohibited conduct.

Application: Nestor peacefully joined the picket line, and the employer identified no violence, obstruction, coercion, property damage, or other illegal act attributable to him. The final judgment against the strike therefore supplies no individual ground for dismissal.

Conclusion: Hence, Nestor's dismissal based solely on peaceful participation in the illegal strike is invalid.

rows.syllabus_topic: Collective Bargaining — Union-security Clause
rows.title: Employer Verification Before Union-security Dismissal
rows.prompt: A valid maintenance-of-membership clause covered employee Sol. The union demanded his dismissal for alleged unpaid dues but attached no ledger or notice. Apex terminated Sol that day without seeking proof or allowing him to answer, although Sol's receipts and the union's own ledger showed full payment. rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. A union-security demand is not self-executing.

Legal Basis: Before dismissing an employee under a union-security clause, the employer must verify that the clause applies, the union's request is proper, sufficient evidence establishes the covered ground, and the employee receives fair notice and an opportunity to respond. Conclusion: Thus, Apex illegally dismissed Sol by enforcing an unverified and factually baseless union demand.

rows.syllabus_topic: Kinds of Employment — Fixed-term Employment
rows.title: Invalid Fixed Terms Used to Defeat Regular Employment
rows.prompt: A food factory hired packer Tess through twenty successive five-month contracts over nine years for work needed every production day. Management imposed preprinted take-it-or-leave-it forms, inserted one-day breaks, and admitted using short terms to avoid regularization and benefits. Tess had no specialized bargaining position or meaningful choice. Are the fixed-term stipulations valid?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The fixed terms unlawfully circumvent security of tenure.

rows.title: Robbery with Rape - Meaning of Rape in Article 294(2)

rows.syllabus_topic: Revised Penal Code, Article 11 - unlawful aggression
rows.title: Self-Defense - Cessation of Unlawful Aggression
rows.prompt: An attacker struck Yuri once with a bottle, then dropped it, raised both empty hands, and backed across the street. Nearly a minute later, without any renewed threat, Yuri took a metal bar, chased the attacker, and broke his arm. Yuri invokes self-defense based on the earlier bottle strike. Was unlawful aggression still present when Yuri used the metal bar?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Unlawful aggression had already ceased.

Legal Basis: Unlawful aggression is the indispensable element of complete or incomplete self-defense. It must be an actual physical assault or an imminent and real threat at the moment defensive force is used. Once the aggressor has disarmed, withdrawn, and no longer presents an actual or imminent danger, later violence is retaliation rather than self-defense.

Application: The attacker dropped the bottle, displayed empty hands, and retreated across the street. Yuri waited nearly a minute, armed himself, and pursued despite the absence of a renewed threat. His later use of force answered a past attack, not an existing or imminent aggression.

Conclusion: Hence, Yuri cannot invoke self-defense for the chase and beating after the danger ended.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the robbery acts committed in furtherance of the conspiracy are attributable to Tomas as a principal.

rows.syllabus_topic: Entrapment and instigation - origin of the criminal design
rows.title: Entrapment - Preexisting Criminal Design
rows.prompt: After verified reports that Dario regularly sold prohibited tablets, an undercover officer asked to buy from him. Dario immediately named his customary price, retrieved his own prepacked tablets, chose the meeting point, and completed the sale for marked money. The officer supplied no drugs and used no pressure. Did the officer instigate the crime?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The officer did not instigate the crime.

Legal Basis: The distinction between instigation and entrapment turns on the source of the criminal design. Instigation exists when law enforcement originates and implants the plan in an otherwise innocent person; entrapment exists when the accused already has the criminal intent and officers merely provide an opportunity to expose it.

Application: Dario immediately named his customary price, produced his own prepacked tablets, chose the meeting point, and completed the sale without pressure from the officer. Those facts show that the criminal design came from Dario, while the officer merely provided the opportunity and marked money.

Conclusion: Hence, the operation was lawful entrapment because Dario supplied the criminal design and tablets while the officer merely offered an opportunity to expose the sale.

The problem also removes any independent offense that would displace the impossible-crime provision.

Conclusion: Hence, Olive is liable for an impossible crime rather than attempted homicide because no living victim existed when she fired.

rows.title: Attempt - Spontaneous Desistance
rows.prompt: Uma pointed a loaded pistol at Vera from a few meters away with intent to kill. Before touching the trigger, and without police intervention, resistance, malfunction, or any other outside cause, Uma reconsidered, lowered the weapon, apologized, and left. No witness movement, police arrival, mechanical failure, or resistance forced her to desist. Her unprompted abandonment was therefore spontaneous, and the problem states no independently completed crime arising from the aiming itself.

Conclusion: Hence, spontaneous desistance prevents conviction for attempted homicide on the stated facts.

rows.prompt: Berto removed a sealed camera from a shop display, concealed it in his backpack, and exercised exclusive control over it before staff stopped him near the exit. rows.title: Conflict of Interest - Directly Adverse Concurrent Representation

rows.title: Electronic Evidence - Duplicate Rule Does Not Prove Authenticity

rows.syllabus_topic: Special Proceedings, Rule 74 - omitted heirs
rows.title: Extrajudicial Settlement - Publication Does Not Bind an Omitted Heir

Conclusion: Wherefore, the settlement cannot prejudice the omitted child's share because publication protects creditors and does not replace an heir's participation or actual notice.

rows.title: Verification - Personal Knowledge or Authentic Records
rows.prompt: Maria signed the verification attached to her complaint and swore that she had read it and that its allegations were true and correct based on her personal knowledge and the authentic contract and payment records she had reviewed. The defendant argues that the complaint must be treated as unverified because some allegations rest on authentic records rather than personal knowledge alone. Is the defendant's objection meritorious?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The defendant's objection is not meritorious.

Legal Basis: Rule 7, Section 4 permits verification by an affidavit that the affiant has read the pleading and that its allegations are true and correct based on personal knowledge or authentic records. The rule states alternative permissible sources of assurance and does not require every verified allegation to rest exclusively on personal recollection.

Application: Maria personally read the complaint and swore to the truth of its allegations using both her own knowledge and the authentic contract and payment records she reviewed. Those are the precise alternative bases recognized by Rule 7, so reliance on records did not defeat verification.

Conclusion: Wherefore, Maria's verification is sufficient because Rule 7 permits allegations sworn true on personal knowledge or authentic records, both of which she expressly invoked.

rows.syllabus_topic: Judicial Ethics - voluntary inhibition for demonstrated bias
rows.title: Judicial Ethics - Adverse Rulings Do Not Establish Bias
rows.prompt: Judge Celia denied a motion to dismiss, later compelled production of records in a reasoned order, and questioned counsel about inconsistent dates while allowing full answers. A party sought voluntary inhibition based only on those adverse rulings and skeptical questions, identifying no extrajudicial statement, personal relationship, financial interest, or arbitrary conduct. Did Judge Celia err in refusing voluntary inhibition?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Judge Celia did not err in refusing voluntary inhibition.

Legal Basis: Voluntary inhibition requires a just or valid reason grounded in an objective showing of bias or prejudice. Bias ordinarily must arise from an extrajudicial source or from judicial conduct clearly demonstrating arbitrariness. Adverse, reviewable rulings and ordinary questioning within the proceedings do not establish partiality by themselves.

Application: Celia explained both challenged rulings and allowed counsel to answer her questions about inconsistent dates. The movant identified no extrajudicial source, personal stake, relationship, or arbitrary act. Its dissatisfaction with reviewable judicial actions therefore supplied no objective basis for recusal.

Conclusion: Thus, Judge Celia properly refused inhibition because the movant showed no extrajudicial bias, personal interest, or arbitrary conduct, and adverse rulings alone do not establish partiality.

rows.syllabus_topic: Evidence, Rule 129, Section 4 - effect of amended pleadings
rows.title: Judicial Admissions - Superseded Pleading
rows.prompt: Yara's original complaint admitted receipt of PHP 400,000, but an admitted amended complaint deleted that allegation and superseded the original. The defendant neither marked nor formally offered the original pleading and nevertheless insists that the deleted statement remains conclusive in the case. Does the superseded allegation retain its status as a conclusive judicial admission without being offered in evidence?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The superseded allegation is no longer a conclusive judicial admission.

Legal Basis: An admitted amended pleading supersedes the original pleading. An allegation deleted from the superseded pleading loses its status as a conclusive judicial admission, although it may still be used as an extrajudicial admission if the original pleading is properly presented and offered in evidence for ordinary evaluation.

Application: The amended complaint displaced Yara's original complaint and omitted the receipt allegation. Because the defendant did not mark or offer the original pleading, the deleted statement was never introduced as an extrajudicial admission and cannot receive conclusive judicial-admission effect.

Conclusion: Hence, the court cannot treat the unoffered superseded allegation as conclusive.

rows.syllabus_topic: Civil Procedure, Rule 35 - genuine issue of material fact
rows.title: Summary Judgment - Unsupported Pleaded Defense
rows.prompt: Evergreen sued Foxline for unpaid deliveries and produced signed receipts. Foxline admitted delivery, price, and nonpayment in deposition but retained a boilerplate answer alleging payment or setoff. After discovery closed, Foxline identified no receipt, offsetting obligation, witness, or admissible record supporting either defense. Do the unsupported allegations alone create a genuine issue that requires a full trial?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The unsupported allegations do not create a genuine issue.

Legal Basis: Rule 35 permits summary judgment when the pleadings, admissions, depositions, affidavits, and other competent materials show no genuine issue of material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. A formal denial or conclusory defense exposed by discovery as unsupported or sham does not require trial.

Application: Foxline admitted the delivery, price, and nonpayment in its deposition, while closed discovery produced no evidence of payment or setoff. Its boilerplate pleading is contradicted by the developed record and supplies no factual dispute that a trial could genuinely resolve.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the court may grant summary judgment on the undisputed debt.

rows.syllabus_topic: Civil Procedure - determination of subject-matter jurisdiction
rows.title: Subject-Matter Jurisdiction - Allegations and Principal Relief Control
rows.prompt: Cedar captioned its complaint as one for damages, but the material allegations assert ownership of agricultural land and the principal relief seeks annulment of the defendant's title and recovery of possession. The damages demand is merely incidental. Can the caption and incidental monetary demand alone determine subject-matter jurisdiction?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The caption and incidental demand do not control jurisdiction.

Legal Basis: Subject-matter jurisdiction is conferred only by law and is determined from the complaint's material allegations, pleaded jurisdictional facts, and principal relief sought, regardless of the caption or defenses. Incidental monetary relief does not change the fundamental nature of an action whose principal object concerns title to or possession of real property.

Application: Cedar's allegations claim ownership, challenge the defendant's title, and principally seek recovery of the land. Because damages are only incidental to that real-property relief, the court must apply the jurisdictional law to the actual allegations and remedy rather than the label damages.

Conclusion: Thus, jurisdiction must follow the complaint's principal real-property relief.

rows.syllabus_topic: Practical Exercises, Rule 110 - attempted homicide Information
rows.title: Information - Allegations for the Attempted Stage
rows.prompt: An Information for attempted homicide alleges the date and place and states that Alex, with intent to kill, thrust a knife toward Ben's chest but did not kill him. It does not allege that Alex failed to perform all acts of execution because of a cause or accident other than his spontaneous desistance. Is the Information sufficient to charge the attempted stage?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The Information does not sufficiently allege the attempted stage.

Legal Basis: Rule 110 requires an Information to state the acts or omissions constituting every essential element of the charged offense. Under Article 6, an attempted felony requires direct commencement by overt acts and nonperformance of all acts of execution because of a cause or accident other than the offender's spontaneous desistance.

Application: The Information alleges homicidal intent and a knife thrust but says only that Ben was not killed. It omits the indispensable circumstance explaining that Alex failed to complete the acts of execution because of an independent cause rather than a voluntary abandonment.

Conclusion: Hence, the Information is insufficient because it omitted the essential allegation that noncompletion resulted from a cause other than Alex's spontaneous desistance.
